title: Main Sources of Indoor Air Pollution at Home
h1: What Are the Main Sources of Indoor Air Pollution?
description: The main sources of indoor air pollution are gas appliances, cooking, cleaning products, mold, dust, pets and outdoor smoke. Learn how each one affects you.
quick_answer: The main sources of indoor air pollution in a home are combustion from gas stoves, furnaces and fireplaces, cooking smoke, cleaning products and other chemicals that release VOCs, mold and moisture, dust, pet dander and dust mites, and outdoor pollution like pollen and wildfire smoke that gets inside. Leaky ducts in attics and garages can also pull dirty air into the system.
body:
Indoor air can carry more pollutants than people expect, because the sources are inside with us and modern homes don't always swap out air quickly. Most sources are easy to identify, and many are easy to reduce once you know about them.

Do gas appliances pollute indoor air?

Yes. Anything that burns fuel releases combustion byproducts. In homes, the main sources are:

  • Gas stoves and ovens, which release nitrogen dioxide and fine particles while cooking
  • Furnaces and water heaters, which should vent outside but can leak if the venting is damaged
  • Fireplaces, both wood and gas
  • Attached garages, where car exhaust can seep into the house

Carbon monoxide is the biggest danger. It has no smell or color. Every home with fuel-burning appliances or an attached garage needs working CO alarms. If a CO alarm sounds, get out and call 911. If you smell gas, leave the house and call the gas utility from outside.

How does cooking affect air quality?

Cooking is one of the largest sources of fine particles in a typical home, whether you cook with gas or electric. Searing, frying and anything that smokes sends particles into the air. Using a range hood that vents outside, and running it during and after cooking, helps a lot. Use the back burners when you can, since hoods capture those better.

What household products release pollutants?

Many everyday products release volatile organic compounds, or VOCs:

  1. Cleaning sprays and disinfectants
  2. Air fresheners, candles and incense
  3. Paints, stains and adhesives
  4. New furniture, cabinets, mattresses and flooring
  5. Personal care products like hairspray and nail polish
  6. Pesticides and stored fuels in garages

Choose low-VOC or fragrance-free products where you can, ventilate while using them, and store paints and chemicals outside the living space.

What role do mold and moisture play?

Mold grows wherever there's ongoing moisture: leaky plumbing, poorly vented bathrooms, damp crawl spaces, roof leaks and AC coils and drain pans. It releases spores and musty-smelling compounds. In Southern California, coastal humidity and bathrooms without good exhaust fans are frequent culprits.

Fixing the moisture is the key. Mold will come back if the water source isn't addressed.

What about dust, pets and allergens?

Household dust is a mix of skin flakes, fibers, dirt, pollen, pet dander and dust mite debris. Pets add dander and saliva proteins that many people react to. Dust mites thrive in bedding and upholstered furniture, especially in humid homes. Regular vacuuming with a HEPA vacuum, washing bedding in hot water, and good HVAC filtration all help.

How does outdoor pollution get inside?

Outdoor air comes in through windows, doors and gaps in the building. In our area, the big outdoor sources are pollen in spring, dust during Santa Ana winds, traffic pollution near busy roads and wildfire smoke.

Your HVAC system can also pull in polluted air. Ducts in most local homes run through the attic, and the equipment often sits in the attic, garage or a hall closet. Leaks on the return side can draw in attic dust, insulation fibers and garage fumes. Sealing those leaks keeps that air out of your rooms.

Older homes add a few more possible sources. Old insulation, aging duct liners and materials from past remodels can shed dust and fibers. If you are planning work on an older home, have suspect materials tested before disturbing them.

How can I reduce indoor air pollution?

  • Vent combustion appliances properly and have them checked regularly
  • Run kitchen and bath exhaust fans that vent outside
  • Upgrade your HVAC filter and change it on schedule
  • Keep humidity between about 30 and 50 percent
  • Seal duct leaks, especially on the return side
  • Use portable HEPA purifiers in bedrooms during smoke events
  • Choose low-VOC products and avoid indoor smoking

faqs: What is the most common indoor air pollutant?

Fine particles from cooking, dust and outdoor sources are among the most common. In homes with gas appliances, nitrogen dioxide from cooking is also common. Good ventilation and filtration help with both.
Can my HVAC system make indoor air worse?
It can if the ducts leak and pull in attic or garage air, if the filter is dirty or poorly fitted, or if the coil and drain pan grow mold. Regular maintenance helps prevent this.
Do air fresheners pollute indoor air?
Many air fresheners release VOCs and fragrance chemicals. Fixing the source of odors and ventilating is a better approach than covering smells up.
How can I tell if my indoor air is polluted?

Signs include lingering odors, visible dust, musty smells, condensation on windows and symptoms that improve when you leave home. An indoor air quality monitor can help you track particles, CO2 and humidity.
